Non-profits lag on technological maturity in India, a new report based on a survey of 500 organisations in the sector said. Even as white collar organisations employing college-educated workers experiment heavily with AI and integrate it into their workflows, non-profits did not score even 50% on digital maturity, even as they showed some interest in using large language models (LLMs) to help with reports and marketing, Delhi-based Digital for Nonprofits (D4NP) said in its State of Nonprofits Digitization Report 2026.

In any industry, D4NP founder and former Google executive Abhinav Chetan said, “nonprofits are always the last, no matter which technological trend you pick … They’re still experimenting. They’re still at level one, by the way — they’re only using it for conversations. They’re not really using it for complicated workflows.”

While AI systems have made it far easier for organisations to do routine work faster, Mr. Chetan said that many were lagging behind on even the earlier digitisation wave. One example the report cited was most organisations not taking advantage of monthly $10,000 ad grants. That came out to millions of dollars of free advertising money simply lying unused.

Of the twenty signals, only one organisation — Child Rights and You (CRY) — was on the right side of digital maturity. Mr. Chetan attributed CRY’s adoption of these tools to the corporate background of its staff. The digital maturity “percolates” due to this factor, Mr. Chetan said.

This doesn’t mean that organisations are not using AI tools at all. Quite the opposite, the report says, pointing out that the majority of Indian startups, six in ten, use at least one AI tool every day, and 85% use more than one AI tool. But on governance and taking advantage of emerging capabilities, most organisations did not score well.

headline: Why is New York City pausing some AI tools in schools? | Explained
body: The Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year
full_body:

“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

“As scientists, it’s very important to invest in the science, to really understand what we know (from) what we don’t know, and investing in fear is not that helpful,” said Joelle Barral, an executive at Google DeepMind and a member of the International Scientific Panel on AI, an independent body.

Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at OpenAI, said in early September that AI developers believed the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. A research engineer who left Google DeepMind in July made similar comments, saying it might already be “too late to avoid” humanity’s eradication by AI.

“We have to change the way we talk about AI risk because for a very long time, it’s either existential and everything is going to die and the killer robots are coming, or it doesn’t really matter,” Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, an investigative reporter, said at the same event, held in New York on September 21 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The International Scientific Panel on AI was created in 2025, with its members selected in February 2026. Its mandate is to advance the scientific understanding of AI and inform UN deliberations. Yoshua Bengio, considered one of the fathers of AI and a co-chair of the panel, said it was important to distinguish between what scientists actually know about AI risks and what can only be “plausibly extrapolated” from that evidence.

Asian equities moved higher across several major markets, with investors tracking the decline in oil prices and expectations of diplomatic progress on the Iran war around the week's UN meeting.

The Hang Seng rose 0.70% to 25,217.40, while Japan's Nikkei gained 1.38% to 65,018.95. Taiwan's index advanced 1.28% to 48,330.46 and South Korea's KOSPI climbed 1.80% to 7,133.97. China's Shanghai Composite rose 0.37% to 3,964.421, while the Shenzhen index gained 0.98% to 13,864.658. Malaysia advanced 0.49% and Singapore's STI rose 0.38%. Australia's ASX 200 gained 0.17%, while New Zealand's NZX 50 slipped 0.01%.

US interest-rate expectations remained a key factor in the global market backdrop after the Federal Reserve raised rates the previous week. Traders were pricing in a 55% chance of a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in October, up from 42.5% a week earlier, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Analysts at ING said the scope to maintain pricing for a more hawkish Fed after the September FOMC remained an argument for further US dollar gains. ING also said it expected both the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve to hike rates in December.

The outlook for global benchmark rates was also reflected in dollar-rupee forward premiums, with traders assessing whether India would follow the global trend of higher benchmark rates as central banks continued to grapple with inflation.

Gold prices declined 0.61% to Rs 1,53,436 per 10 grams for 24-karat gold, while silver was trading at Rs 2,40,200 per kg. The movement in precious metals came alongside broader shifts in financial markets, including changes in oil prices, currencies and expectations around interest rates.

The commodity market was also tracking the easing in crude prices, with Brent moving below the $102-per-barrel mark. Within equities, the decline in oil prices was among the factors supporting investor sentiment. The broader market environment also included expectations around global central-bank rates, with traders assessing the possibility of further rate moves after the US Federal Reserve's latest rate increase.

Rupee ended marginally stronger at 95.8150 per dollar, compared with 95.8725 in the previous session. The currency moved within a narrow range, with lower oil prices and portfolio inflows providing support, while sustained importer hedging demand limited the gains. Inflows linked to the National Stock Exchange of India's IPO also supported rupee, according to traders, while dollar bids from importers, including local oil refiners, kept its appreciation in check.
